# Beyond Dense Transformers: MoE, SSMs, Hybrids {#sec-moe-ssm-hybrids}

@sec-transformer-architecture described a causal decoder with two dense
sublayers: attention mixes positions, and a feed-forward network (FFN)
transforms each position. This chapter varies those two sublayers along
independent axes.

A mixture-of-experts (MoE) FFN stores many expert networks, each a separate
FFN with its own weights, but evaluates only a selected subset for each token.
It changes which parameters a token activates and leaves attention unchanged. A
state-space or linear-recurrent layer changes how the sequence is mixed and
what state is retained during decoding, and leaves the FFN as it was. A hybrid
can use either change, or both, in one stack. Keeping the axes separate
prevents three quantities from being confused: stored parameters, arithmetic
executed for one token, and state retained for one sequence.

## Two independent architecture axes

For a dense Transformer block, every token evaluates the same FFN weights, and
every attention layer retains keys and values for every cached position. That
is one specific design for a language model. The alternatives change it along
two separate axes:

| Axis | Dense choice | Alternative | Resource primarily changed |
|---|---|---|---|
| FFN parameter activation | Evaluate one dense FFN | Route each token through a few experts | Stored parameters relative to expert-path arithmetic |
| Sequence mixing | Attend to cached positions | Update a recurrent state | Work and persistent state as context grows |

These substitutions introduce new costs. MoE routing creates dispatch,
imbalance, and communication. A recurrence compresses history into a state
whose width is fixed by the architecture, so past positions are no longer
individually represented in a growing key-value cache. The comparison therefore
has to be made over a whole workload, counting quality, training arithmetic,
memory, communication, batch shape, and serving latency.

## MoE routes tokens through conditional FFNs

Sparse expert models predate Transformers. Shazeer et al. introduced a
sparsely gated MoE layer at large scale in 2017 inside recurrent language
models [@shazeer2017outrageously]. GShard then combined conditional experts
with Transformer models and automatic sharding [@lepikhin2020gshard], while
Switch Transformer studied top-1 routing and trillion-parameter models
[@fedus2021switch]. The idea these systems share is narrower than their scale
claims. A layer can store more expert weights than one token evaluates.

### Routing is a defined mathematical operation

In one common top-$k$ formulation, used by Mixtral, the first two terms score
and select experts [@jiang2024mixtral]:

$$
z_t=W_rh_t,
\qquad
\mathcal{S}_t=\operatorname{TopK}(z_t,k).
$$

The normalized gate for each selected expert, the weight that scales that
expert's output, is

$$
g_{t,e}=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\exp(z_{t,e})}
{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}_t}\exp(z_{t,j})}, & e\in\mathcal{S}_t,\\[6pt]
0, & e\notin\mathcal{S}_t.
\end{cases}
$$

Each selected expert then contributes to the output:

$$
m_t=\sum_{e=1}^{E}g_{t,e}F_e(h_t).
$$

Here $h_t\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is the hidden vector at token position $t$;
$E$ is the number of routed experts; $W_r\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times d}$ is the
router matrix; $z_{t,e}$ is expert $e$'s routing logit, its unnormalized
score for that token;
$\mathcal{S}_t$ is the set of $k$ selected expert indices;
$g_{t,e}$ is the selected expert's normalized gate weight;
$F_e:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is expert $e$; and
$m_t\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is the MoE output. A residual connection and any
shared expert are outside this equation.

These equations specify one router among several in use. Switch uses top-1
routing; some systems apply softmax before selection, some after it, and some
use sigmoid affinities. The gate value may or may not be renormalized after
top-$k$. These choices change gradients and checkpoint semantics, so a model
description must state them.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-moe-routing
//| fig-cap: "One top-2 MoE path. The router scores all routed experts, selects two, and combines their FFN outputs with gate weights. An optional shared expert is evaluated separately and added without a routed gate."
digraph moe {
  bgcolor="transparent";
  rankdir=TB;
  nodesep=0.32; ranksep=0.42;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1", penwidth=1.1];
  edge [fontsize=9, fontname="Helvetica", color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280"];

  h [label="token state h_t"];
  r [label="router W_r\nE scores"];
  k [label="top-2 selection"];
  e1 [label="routed expert i"];
  e2 [label="routed expert j"];
  idle [label="other experts\nnot evaluated", style="rounded,dashed"];
  mix [label="g_i F_i(h_t) + g_j F_j(h_t)"];
  shared [label="optional shared expert\n(always evaluated)"];
  out [label="MoE output"];

  h -> r -> k;
  k -> e1 [label="g_i"];
  k -> e2 [label="g_j"];
  k -> idle [style=dashed];
  e1 -> mix;
  e2 -> mix;
  h -> shared;
  mix -> out;
  shared -> out [label="add", style=dashed];
}
```

### Stored parameters, selected weights, and runtime are different

Suppose every expert is a bias-free SwiGLU FFN with model width $d$ and expert
hidden width $d_f$. From @sec-transformer-architecture, one expert contains
approximately

$$
P_e=3dd_f
$$

parameters, where $P_e$ counts the gate, value, and down projections; $d$ is
the input and output width; and $d_f$ is the expert's intermediate width.
With $E$ routed experts and no shared expert, the layer stores and evaluates

$$
P_{\mathrm{stored}}=EP_e+Ed,
\qquad
P_{\mathrm{evaluated}}(t)=kP_e+Ed.
$$

Here $Ed$ is the router matrix, whose $E$ scores are all evaluated for token
$t$; $EP_e$ counts every stored expert; and $kP_e$ counts only the selected
expert weights. Biases and always-on block parameters are omitted. Reported
"active parameter" counts often include additional embeddings, attention,
normalization, and shared experts, so the reporting convention must be stated.

@fig-moe-ssm-hybrids-2 evaluates these equations for
$d=4096$, $d_f=14336$, and $k=2$. The selected-expert term stays fixed as
$E$ grows, but the router term grows, and neither line measures wall-clock
time. Runtime also depends on token dispatch, padding or ragged kernels,
all-to-all communication, memory traffic, and the slowest expert shard.

![Stored versus evaluated parameter values for one bias-free SwiGLU MoE layer with model width 4096, expert width 14336, and top-2 routing, on a logarithmic axis. Stored parameters include every expert and the router. Evaluated parameters include two experts and all router scores. The lowest line is the router term $Ed$ alone: it grows with $E$, but at 64 experts it is still under 0.1 percent of the evaluated count, which is why that line looks flat. Attention and other always-on weights are excluded.](/figures/moe-ssm-hybrids-2.svg){#fig-moe-ssm-hybrids-2}

The runnable cell prints the same accounting without requiring plotting
libraries. Change $E$, $k$, or either width to inspect another layer.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
model_width = 4096
expert_width = 14_336
selected_experts = 2

def moe_parameter_counts(experts):
    if not 1 <= selected_experts <= experts:
        raise ValueError("selected_experts must be between 1 and experts")
    per_expert = 3 * model_width * expert_width  # bias-free SwiGLU
    router = experts * model_width
    stored = experts * per_expert + router
    evaluated = selected_experts * per_expert + router
    return stored, evaluated

for experts in (8, 16, 32, 64):
    stored, evaluated = moe_parameter_counts(experts)
    print(
        f"E={experts:2d}, k={selected_experts}: "
        f"stored={stored / 1e9:.3f}B, "
        f"evaluated/token={evaluated / 1e9:.3f}B, "
        f"ratio={stored / evaluated:.2f}x"
    )
```
::::

### Routing creates a dispatch problem

Expert weights are commonly partitioned across an expert-parallel group, a set
of devices that each hold a subset of the experts. A forward pass then has four
stages: compute router scores, group token copies by destination expert,
exchange those copies to the expert owners, and return the expert outputs to
their original token order. Implementations often use one
all-to-all collective for dispatch and another for the return path, but an
all-to-all is not intrinsic when all experts are local or the placement differs.

The arithmetic saved inside expert FFNs can therefore be replaced by network
time or small, poorly utilized matrix multiplications. Useful measurements
include bytes dispatched, tokens per expert, padded versus useful expert slots,
collective time, overlap with computation, and tail latency. None of these can
be derived from the active-parameter count.

For a routing group with $T$ tokens, $E$ experts, and $k$ assignments per token,
the even-share load is $kT/E$ assignments per expert. A fixed-capacity
implementation may reserve

$$
C_e=\left\lceil c\frac{kT}{E}\right\rceil
$$

slots per expert, where $c>0$ is the capacity factor; $C_e$ is the assignment
capacity of expert $e$; $T$ is the number of tokens in the routing group; $kT$
is the total number of routed assignments; and $E$ is the expert count. An
overflow policy may skip, reroute, or defer assignments. Switch's published
formula is the $k=1$ case [@fedus2021switch]. Other systems use dropless ragged
or block-sparse execution instead of a fixed cap [@gale2023megablocks].

```{figure}
//| figure: moe-dispatch
//| label: fig-moe-ssm-hybrids-moe-routing
//| fig-cap: "One routing group of 24 tokens dispatched to $E$ experts with top-$k$ routing, one assignment per step: in token order, every token's first choice claims a slot before any second choice. Each expert has $C_e=\lceil c\,kT/E\rceil$ slots. An assignment that finds its expert full is dropped, so it contributes nothing and a token that loses every assignment leaves the layer on its residual path, or, with rerouting, it goes to the token's best-scoring unselected expert that still has a free slot. The token panel follows one token through $p_t$, $\mathcal{S}_t$, and $g_{t,e}$. The chart reruns the whole group at every capacity factor, so dropped assignments and empty slots move in opposite directions. Router logits are seeded illustrative values; the router-load setting adds a per-expert bias to them. The balance term is Switch's $E\sum_e f_eq_e$ from the next section."
```

### Balance losses shape optimization

Unregularized routing can concentrate assignments, under-train some experts,
and make overloaded expert ranks into stragglers. Shazeer et al. used separate
importance and load objectives [@shazeer2017outrageously]. Switch introduced a
simpler top-1 auxiliary loss, an extra term added to the training loss:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bal}}
=\alpha E\sum_{e=1}^{E}f_eq_e,
\qquad
f_e=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}
\mathbf{1}\!\left[\arg\max_j p_{t,j}=e\right],
\qquad
q_e=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}p_{t,e}.
$$

Here $p_t=\operatorname{softmax}(z_t)$ is the full router distribution for
token $t$; $f_e$ is the realized fraction of tokens sent to expert $e$;
$q_e$ is its mean router probability; $T$ is the routing-group token count;
$E$ is the expert count; $\alpha\ge0$ is the loss coefficient; and
$\mathbf{1}[\cdot]$ is an indicator. The product penalizes jointly large
traffic and probability mass. Top-$k$ systems use related but not identical
definitions.

The coefficient sets the balance between two failure modes. Too little balance
pressure can leave experts poorly utilized, while too much can override
task-driven routing.
DeepSeek-V3 primarily steers top-$k$ selection with per-expert biases that are
adjusted from recent load, while retaining a small sequence-wise auxiliary
loss to prevent extreme imbalance [@deepseek2024deepseekv3;
@wang2024auxiliaryfree]. The bias affects selection, not the gate weight used
to combine expert outputs. Describing the model as having removed all
balancing losses is therefore inaccurate.

ST-MoE also introduced a router z-loss, a penalty that keeps router logits from
growing large [@zoph2022stmoe]:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{z}
=\frac{\beta}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}
\left(\log\sum_{e=1}^{E}\exp z_{t,e}\right)^2.
$$

Here $z_{t,e}$ is the router logit defined earlier; the log-sum-exp term is the
router log-partition for token $t$; $T$ and $E$ retain their earlier meanings;
and $\beta\ge0$ controls the penalty. Switch also reported selectively using
float32 for router computations inside a model otherwise computed in the
16-bit bfloat16 format [@fedus2021switch]. Both are stabilizers supported by
experiments. Neither result shows that hard top-$k$ selection or low precision
causes every MoE failure.

### Refinements solve different routing problems

Each of the following designs addresses a different routing problem, and they
coexist as alternatives:

- **Top-1 and top-$k$.** Switch evaluates one expert; Mixtral evaluates two.
  Increasing $k$ raises expert arithmetic and communication, approaching dense
  expert evaluation only as $k$ approaches $E$.
- **Expert-choice and balanced assignment.** Expert Choice gives each expert a
  fixed token bucket, eliminating expert-side overflow but giving tokens a
  variable number of selected experts, possibly zero [@zhou2022expert]. BASE
  Layers instead formulate routing as a balanced assignment problem
  [@lewis2021base].
- **Fine-grained and shared experts.** DeepSeekMoE divides expert capacity into
  smaller routed experts and adds always-evaluated shared experts
  [@dai2024deepseekmoe]. In that construction, shared outputs are added without
  a routed gate. The paper reports improved specialization in its experiments;
  the label "shared" does not guarantee that a network has learned only general
  knowledge.
- **Sparse upcycling.** A dense FFN can be copied into several experts, followed
  by continued training with a new router [@komatsuzaki2022sparse]. Upcycling
  affects only the initialization cost; the resulting model has the dispatch
  and serving behavior of any MoE model with the same configuration.

GLaM and Mixtral demonstrate other points in the design space
[@du2022glam; @jiang2024mixtral]. Their results do not establish a universal
best expert count, $k$, capacity factor, or routing loss. Those values depend on
the training budget, batch shape, topology, memory, kernels, and target latency.

## State-space layers replace a growing history with a recurrence

The second axis concerns sequence mixing. A state-space model (SSM) carries a
fixed-size state vector: each input updates it, and each output is read from
it. SSMs originate in dynamical-systems and control formulations, long before
their use in neural sequence models. S4 showed in 2022 that a structured
linear state-space layer could model long sequences efficiently [@gu2021s4].
Mamba then made key parts of the recurrence input-dependent and supplied a
hardware-aware selective scan [@gu2023mamba].

### From a continuous system to a discrete layer

A linear time-invariant state-space system is

$$
\frac{dh(t)}{dt}=Ah(t)+Bx(t),
\qquad
y(t)=Ch(t)+D_{\mathrm{skip}}x(t).
$$

Here continuous time is $t$; $x(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}}$ is the input;
$h(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the state; $y(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}}$ is the
output; $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ is the state transition;
$B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{in}}$ writes the input into state;
$C\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times n}$ reads the state; and
$D_{\mathrm{skip}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times d_{in}}$ is a direct input
path. The dimensions $d_{in}$, $n$, and $d_{out}$ are fixed by the layer.

Discretization replaces the continuous derivative with one update per token
position. After discretization at a fixed step, the same layer can be written

$$
h_t=\bar A h_{t-1}+\bar Bx_t,
\qquad
y_t=Ch_t+D_{\mathrm{skip}}x_t.
$$

Here integer $t$ is a token position; $x_t$, $h_t$, and $y_t$ are the sampled
input, state, and output; and $\bar A$ and $\bar B$ are the discretized
transition and input matrices. They are not the continuous matrices $A$ and
$B$, even when an implementation derives them from those parameters.

### Fixed coefficients give recurrence-convolution equivalence

With $h_0=0$ and fixed $\bar A$, $\bar B$, and $C$, the terms in the unrolled
recurrence are

$$
K_i=C\bar A^{i}\bar B,
\qquad
y_t=\sum_{j=1}^{t}K_{t-j}x_j+D_{\mathrm{skip}}x_t.
$$

Here $i\ge0$ is a lag; $K_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times d_{in}}$ is the
convolution kernel at that lag; $\bar A^i$ is the $i$-th matrix power; $j$ is
an earlier token position; and all other symbols retain their definitions
above. The recurrent and convolutional views compute the same linear operator.
S4 exploits structure in $A$ to generate and apply long kernels efficiently.
Its filter generation and FFT steps carry their own costs, so the statement
that every SSM implementation is $O(S)$ in sequence length $S$ is too coarse.

### Mamba makes the recurrence selective

For one simplified Mamba channel, a single feature dimension with its own
recurrent state, the token-dependent terms produced by the selection mechanism
are

$$
(\Delta_t,B_t,C_t)=s_\theta(x_t),
\qquad
\bar A_t=\exp(\Delta_tA),
\qquad
\bar B_t=
\int_{0}^{\Delta_t}\exp\!\bigl((\Delta_t-\tau)A\bigr)B_t\,d\tau.
$$

These terms define the discrete recurrence:

$$
h_t=\bar A_th_{t-1}+\bar B_tx_t,
\qquad
y_t=C_th_t+D_{\mathrm{skip}}x_t.
$$

Here $s_\theta$ is a learned projection with parameters $\theta$;
$\Delta_t>0$ is an input-dependent discretization step; $B_t$ and $C_t$ are
input-dependent write and read maps; $A$ remains a learned but
input-independent continuous transition; $\exp$ is the matrix exponential;
$\tau$ is the integration variable; and $\bar A_t$ and $\bar B_t$ are the
token-dependent discrete maps. Production Mamba layers batch many channels and
use structured parameterizations, but the distinction is the same:
$\Delta_t$, $B_t$, and $C_t$ are selective; continuous $A$ is not
[@gu2023mamba].

Input dependence removes the single stationary convolution kernel $K$ from the
previous section. Mamba recovers parallel training through a fused associative
scan, a parallel prefix computation, over affine recurrence updates, then uses
the recurrent form for autoregressive decoding. Mamba-2 relates a restricted
class of SSM transitions to semiseparable mixing matrices, structured
matrices whose submatrices in the lower-triangular part have low rank, and
uses chunked matrix multiplication; its paper reports a 2 to 8 times faster
core layer than Mamba's selective scan in the tested settings
[@dao2024mamba2]. That is a measured result under those
implementations, not an architecture-independent speed ratio.

### Linear attention is another fixed-state route

Kernelized causal attention can also reorder its computation into a recurrent
state. A simplified gated form is

$$
S_t=\lambda_tS_{t-1}+\phi(k_t)v_t^{\top},
\qquad
z_t=\lambda_tz_{t-1}+\phi(k_t),
\qquad
y_t=\frac{\phi(q_t)^{\top}S_t}
{\phi(q_t)^{\top}z_t+\varepsilon}.
$$

Here $q_t$, $k_t$, and $v_t$ are query, key, and value vectors;
$\phi$ is a feature map that makes the kernel factorable;
$S_t$ is a fixed-shape key-value summary matrix; $z_t$ is its normalizer state;
$\lambda_t\in[0,1]$ is an optional learned forgetting gate;
$\varepsilon>0$ prevents division by zero; and $y_t$ is the output. The
associative factorization, not merely removing softmax, eliminates the need to
form every query-key pair. Gated DeltaNet adds targeted delta-rule updates to
this family [@yang2024gateddeltanet].

### Sequence-length growth and decode state

With model dimensions fixed, dense full-sequence attention forms a number of
query-key relationships proportional to $S^2$, while a recurrent scan performs
a number of state updates proportional to $S$. @fig-moe-ssm-hybrids-1 plots
only that sequence-length growth, normalized at 1,000 tokens. It does not plot
FLOPs or measured runtime; projection width, state size, kernel fusion, memory
traffic, and hardware determine the constants.

![Growth of the dominant sequence-length term, normalized at a 1,000-token context. Dense attention relationships grow quadratically with context length; recurrent state updates grow linearly when model dimensions are fixed. The curves are asymptotic accounting, not a runtime benchmark.](/figures/moe-ssm-hybrids-1.svg){#fig-moe-ssm-hybrids-1}

During decode, one dense attention layer compares a new query with a retained
key for each cached position. A recurrent layer instead updates a state whose
shape is independent of context length. "Independent of context length" does
not mean small or free. In the original Mamba implementation, a useful
approximation for persistent decode state is

$$
M_{\mathrm{rec}}
=B_{\mathrm{batch}}L_{\mathrm{rec}}d_{\mathrm{inner}}
\bigl(n_{\mathrm{state}}+d_{\mathrm{conv}}\bigr)b
\quad\text{bytes}.
$$

Here $B_{\mathrm{batch}}$ is the number of resident sequences;
$L_{\mathrm{rec}}$ is the number of recurrent layers;
$d_{\mathrm{inner}}$ is the number of recurrent channels;
$n_{\mathrm{state}}$ is the SSM state width per channel;
$d_{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the short-convolution buffer length; and $b$ is bytes
per stored element. Exact layouts vary by implementation. The state scales
with batch, layers, channel width, state width, convolution width, and
precision, but not with cached context length.

```{figure}
//| figure: recurrent-state
//| label: fig-moe-ssm-hybrids-ssm-vs-attention
//| fig-cap: "Twenty-four tokens, four content digits among filler, read by an attention layer and by one channel and one state dimension of a selective recurrence with $A=-1$. The attention layer appends one KV record per token and keeps it unchanged. The recurrent state holds one number per state dimension, so the bars show the weight each earlier input still has in it, $w_{t,j}=\bar B_j\prod_{i=j+1}^{t}\bar A_i$ with $\bar A_i=\exp(\Delta_iA)$. With a fixed $\Delta$, every token, filler included, multiplies what came before by the same $\exp(-\Delta)$. With a selective $\Delta_t$, filler tokens take a small step that leaves the state almost unchanged, and each content token shrinks what came before by $\exp(-\Delta)$ as it writes. The $\Delta_t$ values are illustrative, not taken from a trained model, and the weights describe how the state mixes inputs, not how well a trained model recalls them. A full layer has $d_{\mathrm{inner}}\times n_{\mathrm{state}}$ such dimensions; the byte counts use Jamba v0.1's layer shapes in bf16."
```

The two mechanisms also represent history differently. Attention retains a
separate cached representation for each past position and permits direct
content-based access.
A recurrent layer repeatedly compresses prior information into a fixed-shape
state, so information can interfere or be lost. Neither mechanism guarantees
recall. Retrieval quality must be measured on the target distribution, at the
target length, after matched training.

## Hybrids choose a layer schedule

MoE and recurrent sequence mixing compose because they occupy different block
slots. A hybrid may use attention in some layers, a recurrence in others, and
either dense or expert FFNs after each mixer. There is no required ratio.

```{figure}
//| figure: hybrid-schedule
//| label: fig-moe-hybrid-stack
//| fig-cap: "A 32-layer stack with Jamba v0.1's layer shapes and the two schedule fields set independently. The mixer row chooses attention or Mamba for each layer and sets the state one sequence keeps while it decodes: $2SH_{kv}d_hb$ bytes per attention layer, which grows with the context length $S$, and $d_{\mathrm{inner}}(n_{\mathrm{state}}+d_{\mathrm{conv}})b$ per Mamba layer, which does not. The FFN row chooses expert or dense FFNs and changes only the stored and evaluated FFN parameters. Values follow the chapter's equations in bf16. Schedules other than Jamba's reuse the same layer shapes and are not released models. The rings mark the KV cache sizes the Jamba paper reports at 256K tokens [@lieber2024jamba]."
```

Released models illustrate different schedules and reporting conventions:

| Model | Sequence mixers | FFN sparsity | Scope of the reported evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jamba | One attention layer per seven Mamba layers in its main configuration | 16 experts, top-2 in selected layers | The authors report stronger throughput and lower KV memory than named baselines under specified hardware and context settings [@lieber2024jamba] |
| MiniMax-01 | Seven Lightning Attention (linear-attention) blocks per softmax-attention block | 32 experts, top-2; 456B total and 45.9B activated | The report trained to 1M-token contexts and evaluated extrapolation to 4M [@minimax2025minimax01] |
| Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B | Twelve repetitions of three Gated DeltaNet layers and one gated-attention layer | 512 routed experts, 10 selected, plus one shared expert | The official card reports 80B total, 3B activated, and a native 262,144-token context [@qwen2025qwen3next] |
| Nemotron-H | Mamba-2, attention, and dense FFN layers | Dense FFNs | The authors report 8B, 56B, and distilled 47B variants, with throughput comparisons scoped to their benchmark setup [@nvidia2025nemotronh] |

These examples establish that the components can be trained and implemented at
large scale. They leave open whether a hybrid outperforms full attention on a
given quality measure or serving workload. MiniMax later chose full attention
for M2
and reported that hybrid weaknesses appeared on complex multi-hop tasks at
larger scale, while low-precision state, prefix caching, speculative decoding,
kernel maturity, and evaluation remained practical concerns
[@minimax2025m2attention]. That retrospective reports one team's first-party
evidence and is not a general result about recurrent or hybrid models.

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested

The open question is where the quality, state capacity, and implementation
costs of subquadratic mixers cross the full-attention baseline for a particular
workload. Small or saturated benchmarks can hide retrieval and multi-step
reasoning deficits; theoretical linear work can still be memory-bound; and an
attention-heavy software stack may erase an architecture's nominal advantage.
Comparisons need matched data, tokens, parameters, training compute, kernels,
hardware, context lengths, and serving features.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow

The architecture fixes two sets of requirements for @sec-training-at-scale.
MoE fixes expert placement, dispatch volume, and load imbalance across the device
topology. Recurrent and hybrid mixers fix scan kernels, state precision, and
which layers still allocate a KV cache. Those choices then constrain batching,
prefix reuse, speculative decoding, and memory scheduling in
@sec-serving-problem. An asymptotic saving is useful only if the distributed
and serving implementations can realize it.
:::

## Record sparse and recurrent architecture as a contract

A reproducible architecture description should name at least:

- which layers use attention, an SSM, linear attention, or another mixer;
- every attention mask, head layout, position rule, and KV-cache data type;
- recurrent state shapes, discretization or gate parameterization,
  convolution width, reset semantics, and state precision;
- expert count, shared-expert count, selected routed experts, expert FFN
  shapes, and which layers are sparse;
- router scoring, normalization, top-$k$ tie-breaking, gate renormalization,
  and output-combination rule;
- balance and z-loss equations with coefficients, plus any bias-update rule;
- routing-group size, capacity factor, overflow or dropless policy, and token
  ordering after combine;
- expert placement, expert-parallel group, dispatch collective, router
  precision, and reported total/activated-parameter convention.

Names such as "MoE," "Mamba hybrid," or "80B-A3B" leave most of this contract
undefined. Checkpoint tensors, training code, inference kernels, and model cards
must agree on it.

## Validate each axis before scaling

1. **Check parameter accounting.** Reconcile stored, selected, shared, router,
   and always-on parameters with the serialized checkpoint.
2. **Test routing exactly.** On a small batch, compare sharded dispatch and
   combine with a single-device reference, including ties, overflow, padding,
   and zero-token experts.
3. **Measure the load distribution.** Report assignments per expert, imbalance,
   dropped or rerouted assignments, padding, entropy, and the slowest expert
   rank over training and evaluation data.
4. **Measure communication.** Record dispatch and combine bytes, collective
   time, compute overlap, and end-to-end tokens per second at realistic batch
   sizes.
5. **Compare scan and recurrence.** Confirm the parallel training path and
   token-by-token recurrent path agree within declared numerical tolerances.
6. **Test state boundaries.** Reset state at document and sequence boundaries;
   test packed samples, prefix reuse, state copying, and speculative rollback.
7. **Stress retrieval and state tracking.** Evaluate direct lookup, order,
   repeated keys, distractors, and multi-hop use across the deployed length,
   rather than relying on one needle test, which retrieves a single planted
   fact.
8. **Benchmark the complete workload.** Compare quality, training throughput,
   prefill, decode, memory, batch capacity, and failure recovery against dense
   and attention-only baselines under matched budgets.

MoE and recurrent layers each remove one dense assumption, and both still
require resource accounting. The architecture contract records that
accounting: which weights a token evaluates, where those weights live, how
sequence state evolves, and which costs move into communication or serving.
